summary:
Pluto was found by blinking two photographs of the same patch of sky. NASA's SPHEREx now photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colours every six months, far too much to blink by hand. Planetes turns any position on the sky into a SPHEREx time-lapse: type coordinates or pick one of the five challenge targets, and the available real SPHEREx exposures of that spot play like a short film on one shared brightness scale, with SPHEREx's own quality flags. Stars that move, brighten or fade stand out at once.

For an object, Planetes then forms two complementary opinions: how it moves, and what its light says. The spectrum gives a type and a distance; with the motion that gives a speed that either makes sense or does not, and Planetes says which and why. It blinks a real asteroid exactly where JPL predicts it, and a Planet X calculator shows how bright a distant planet would look to SPHEREx. Every image and number is real archive data, every result is checked against known answers on a public Validation page, and it runs in any browser with nothing to install.
details:
Try it: planetes.divergit.com · Code: github.com/nova-rishabh/Planetes

What it does

  • Time-lapse of any sky position from the available SPHEREx visits, aligned north-up on one shared brightness scale, with SPHEREx's quality flags and each frame's detector and wavelength. The five challenge targets (Barnard's Star, ε Indi B, WISE 0855, R Draconis, RW Aurigae) play instantly.
  • Blink comparator, the method that found Pluto, plus stack, difference and colour views that make faint motion and colour changes visible.
  • A real mover: two SPHEREx frames of asteroid 1562 Gondolatsch, 3.2 hours apart, sit within 0.11 pixels of where JPL predicts it from SPHEREx's own position. The same check finds 15 of 17 known asteroids in 20 ecliptic fields.
  • Catalogue stars from Gaia DR3 and AllWISE moved to each frame's date, and a sky-context map.
  • Spectrum from 0.75 to 5 µm built from SPHEREx's own pixels, with every rejected point explained.
  • Two Opinions: the spectrum is matched to standard brown-dwarf and star spectra (ε Indi B: type T3 at 2.55–3.69 pc vs 3.64 pc from Gaia), and the verdict says Agree, Disagree or Can't tell, with reasons.
  • Planet X calculator: brightness in SPHEREx bands and the six-month jump for any distance and size.
  • Validation page: every measurement checked against a known answer, e.g. Barnard's Star motion within 1.6 % of Gaia.
  • Shareable links with coordinates in the URL, an embeddable view, a guided tour and a sound mode.

How it works

A Python pipeline asks the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) for the SPHEREx exposures covering the position (Data Release 1 and Quick Releases 2–3), downloads small cutouts, subtracts the zodiacal light, aligns each frame to the sky and renders all frames with one shared stretch. Forced photometry in every frame builds the spectrum; a spectral typer and an asteroid thermometer turn it into a distance, and a verdict engine compares it with the motion. A FastAPI service runs these jobs and a Next.js site plays them. Every number keeps its SPHEREx observation ID, and the site keeps working through archive outages.

Benefits and impact

Anyone — a student, a citizen scientist, a teacher — can see how the infrared sky changes in seconds, and learn why a "change" can be a moving star, a variable star or an instrument glitch. It brings the WiseView-style blink search that found hundreds of brown dwarfs in WISE data to SPHEREx's 102 colours.

Creativity

It pairs two complementary lines of evidence, motion and colour, and only calls something interesting when they agree. It publishes its own test results, including the honest Can't tell answers.

Tools

Python (Astropy, astroquery, pyvo, photutils, NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI) · TypeScript (Next.js, React, three.js) · Aladin Lite · hosted on Vercel and Render.

Factors we considered

  • Saturated pixels are never used in a verdict.
  • SPHEREx pixels are about 6″, so we do not claim parallax.
  • Claims are worded "consistent with", never "discovered".
  • Every source is credited; see References.

Status and what's next

Six of ten validation tests pass: Barnard's Star motion (within 1.6 % of Gaia), ε Indi B type and distance, known asteroids (15 of 17), saturated variables, false-alarm control and a clean re-run. Four are scripted, with their pass rules fixed in advance, but not yet run: ε Indi B and WISE 0855 motion from positions measured in each frame (V2, V3), our photometry against IRSA's (V4), and the asteroid thermometer on real asteroids (V7). They need NASA/IPAC IRSA's SPHEREx search service, which has been returning errors ("502 Proxy Error") on IRSA's own servers for every user. The site handles this openly: it says when the archive is down, explains what failed, and shows a backup SPHEREx all-sky map from NASA's open-data copy. The four tests run as soon as the service answers, and their results go on the Validation page whether they pass or not.
